Alright, I've just finished a series of critical updates: added a “reality nudge” guard in `agent.ts` to catch fabricated action claims, introduced a regex helper `claimsAction` in the same file, tightened the prompt wording to forbid invented tool results, and modified `tools.ts` so that any non‑zero exit code now throws an error rather than silently returning output. I also lowered the default temperature in `groq.ts` to make the model more deterministic.

Given these changes, I need to validate that the new safeguards are actually effective. The last test I ran (the “stats.sh” script) succeeded, but I executed it via `bash stats.sh`. That bypasses the executable flag and also doesn't test the new error‑propagation behavior, because the `bash` tool wrapper would capture the exit code and I haven’t yet verified that a thrown error surfaces correctly. Moreover, I want to ensure that the guard doesn't mistakenly allow a fabricated claim when the model says it created or edited a file but no tool actually did so.

So the next logical step is to re‑run the same complex task, but this time:
1. Remove any existing `stats.sh` to start clean.
2. Invoke the Glint CLI with the same prompt, but phrase it to ask for the “real output” (so the guard will trigger if the model tries to claim the script ran without actually running it).
3. Use `--yolo` to bypass any manual approvals, since I’m in an automated test.
4. After the run, capture the tail of the CLI output (a few more lines than before – `-18` instead of `-15`) to make sure I see any guard messages.
5. Verify that `stats.sh` exists and is executable (`ls -la stats.sh`).
6. Finally, run the script directly with `./stats.sh /etc` (not via `bash`) to test that the executable flag works and that any non‑zero exit codes are correctly thrown and reported by the new error handling in `tools.ts`.

All of this can be done with a single Bash tool call. I’ll change the working directory to `/tmp/glint-test`, clean up the old script, run the Glint CLI with the appropriate prompt, pipe the output through `tail -18`, then print a verification header, list the script file, and execute it directly. This will give me a clear picture of whether the fabrication guard and error propagation are functioning as intended.

Thus, I’ll issue the following Bash command:
